title: Predictive queue model for microbatch shaping and KV-memory forecasting
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Problem statement:
High-QPS tail events cause oscillation in microbatch thresholds and noisy KV-cache evictions. Current admission controller uses instantaneous headroom heuristics (free_gpu_mem / reserve), which reacts late and produces transient overloads: longer tail latency, KV churn and repeated cold-cache misses. We need a predictive controller that forecasts short-term queue growth and KV working set pressure to shape admission and issue soft backpressure before memory scarcity worsens.

Goals:
- Reduce P95/P99 generation latency spikes during 5–30s traffic surges by 25% relative to baseline.
- Reduce KV-cache churn (evictions/sec) during spikes by 30% and cold-cache miss ratio by 20%.
- Keep overall throughput within 3% of current baseline when no spike occurs.

Proposed approach:
1) Build a lightweight predictive queue model running in inference router that consumes (per-shard): recent arrival rate (1s/5s/15s EWMA), microbatch fill rate, outstanding inflight tokens, and KV-access hotness summary. Model outputs: 5s and 15s forecast for queued request count and expected KV working set growth (MB). Implementation choices: simple time-series exponential smoothing + AR(1) with traffic class stratification. As a future step swap to a small GRU if needed.

2) Use forecast to compute two actionable signals every 200ms: predicted_headroom_short (MB) and predicted_queue_delta. Admission logic uses a three-way decision: allow / preferential-defer / soft-backpressure. Preferential-defer is a low-latency path for high-priority tokens (interactive) while deferring low-priority batchable requests. Soft-backpressure emits a 503-with-retry-after or a 429-defer token depending on caller contract.

3) Tie KV cache prefetch and eviction policy to predicted_working_set_delta: when forecast shows growth > X MB in 15s, switch eviction to LRU-2 with conservative compaction, and pre-emptively spill less-hot shards to host RAM (or trigger async quantized checkpointing).

4) Safety knobs and fallbacks: keep existing static headroom floor (configurable per-pool), an exponential backoff guard to avoid oscillatory admission toggles, and conservative decay window for forecasts. We’ll expose tuning params in Redwood Console for dedicated pools.

Why this is different from past efforts:
- Past tickets focused on reactive thresholds and slot-level heuristics. This ticket moves to short-horizon forecasting and preferential-defer gating to protect interactive latency without aggressive global throttles.
- Emphasizes KV-policy coupling (eviction / spill / prefetch) driven by forecasts rather than purely reactive memory pressure flags.

Risks and trade-offs:
- Forecasting errors could under- or over-trigger backpressure; mitigation includes conservative thresholds, runbooked kill-switch, and small canary rollout.
- Prefetch/spill actions add complexity and could increase I/O; we will bound I/O bandwidth during spikes and prefer in-memory compaction first.

Success metrics (measured during canary):
- P95 generation latency under synthetic 2x baseline QPS ramp reduced by >=25%
- Evictions/sec reduced by >=30% during ramp
- Cold-cache miss ratio delta reduced by >=20%
- No more than 3% reduction in sustained throughput in normal traffic

Acceptance criteria:
- Predictive model runs at <2% CPU overhead on router host at 99th percentile of sampling rate.
- Admission decisions are deterministic for a given forecast seed and traffic trace (replayable in test harness).
- Automated integration test that replays recorded spike traces validates P95/P99 budget improvements.

Operational playbook (short):
- Canary rollout to 5% of serving routers in region us-west-2 for 48h, monitor latency and evictions.
- If P99 regresses >5% or evictions increase >10% open rollback and increase safefloor.
- After success, ramp to 25% then 100% over 14 days.
